draft.title: Stages of learning
card: Cognitive
the learner thinks through each step of the skill. Movements are jerky, errors are large and frequent, and the learner needs clear instructions.
Associative
the learner practises and refines the skill. Errors become smaller and fewer, movements are smoother, and the learner starts to spot and fix their own mistakes.
Autonomous
the skill is automatic. The learner can perform it smoothly and consistently without thinking about each step, so attention is free for other things such as tactics.
Learners move through the stages in order, at different speeds. Moving on depends on how much quality practice they have had.
draft.remember: Think it through, then refine it, then do it without thinking.

a.q: Which description fits a learner in the associative stage?
opts: Movements are smoother and errors are starting to be self-fixed
Movements are jerky and each step is thought through
The skill is automatic and the learner can focus on tactics
The learner cannot yet tell when an error has been made
a.why: In the associative stage the learner refines the skill, with smaller errors and some ability to self-correct. Thinking through each step is the cognitive stage, and automatic performance is the autonomous stage.
a.clue: This is the middle stage, between thinking and automatic.

b.q: Ayesha has played netball for years. In a match she passes smoothly without thinking about her hands, and instead reads where her teammates are moving. Which stage is she in, and why?
opts: Autonomous, because the pass is automatic and frees attention
Associative, because she is still refining how she passes
Cognitive, because she has to think about where players move
Autonomous, because she makes no errors at all when passing
b.why: Her pass needs no conscious thought, so her attention is free for tactics. That is the autonomous stage. Thinking about teammates is a tactical choice, not thinking through the steps of the pass, and the autonomous stage does not mean the learner never makes an error.
b.clue: Where is her attention while she passes?
